name: Eritrea
headline: Eritrea has no data protection law and mostly paper records; doctors face prison for revealing secrets, but patients have no verified right to their records.

access.summary: We found no legal right for a patient to see or copy their medical record: the 2015 Civil Code's medical contract chapter is silent on records, and any such rule in other health proclamations is not verified. There is no patient portal.
detail: The 2015 Civil Code sets out medical and hospital contracts (Articles 2332 to 2345) covering fees and liability, but gives no right to see or copy a record.
Eritrea has no data protection law, so there is no general right of access to personal data either.
The 1997 Constitution promises a right to privacy, but it was ratified and never came into effect.
Studies describe patient histories kept on paper clinical cards in facilities.

control.summary: The Civil Code lets a person refuse treatment and stop a professional revealing what they confided. Beyond that, no consent choices, opt-out or access log for health records were found, and data runs to a ministry system.
detail: Civil Code Article 20 lets a person refuse a medical examination or treatment, except compulsory vaccination and similar public-interest measures.
Article 23 says a person who confided facts to a professional may ensure they are not revealed.
The Penal Code allows disclosure when the person expressly authorises it, or when a law, court or other competent authority orders it.
There is no data protection law, so no rules on consent to processing or sharing exist.

privacy.summary: A medical professional who discloses a patient's secret commits a crime carrying one to three years in prison under the 2015 Penal Code. But Eritrea has no data protection law, no regulator and no breach rules.
detail: Penal Code Article 145 punishes disclosure of professional secrets by medical professionals with one to three years. Negligent disclosure carries six to twelve months or a fine of 20,001 to 50,000 Nakfa.
Disclosure ordered by a law, court or other competent authority is not an offence, a wide state exception.
Unauthorised use of a computer is an offence, aggravated for public institutions.
No data protection authority exists, and Law Lab Africa found no enforcement as of September 2026.
Eritrea has no EU adequacy decision, so EU data sent there needs GDPR transfer safeguards.

commercial.summary: No law limits selling health data or using it for marketing, because Eritrea has no data protection law. The only protection found is the Penal Code's secrecy offence, with a heavier sentence for disclosure for gain.
detail: Penal Code Article 146 sets three to five years for breach of confidence committed for monetary or other gain. Its cross-reference reads Article 139, which appears to mean Article 145 (not verified).
The Civil Code bars selling a person's image without consent, but nothing covers health data sales, brokers or apps.
No rules on de-identified data sales were found.

journey.summary: The Ministry of Health collects aggregate facility reports through DHIS2, which connected 342 facilities in 2018, mostly offline. Patient records do not follow people between clinics, hospitals and pharmacies.
detail: The 2010 National Health Policy plans an automated health data repository at central and zoba (regional) levels.
In 2018 the Ministry of Information reported DHIS2 in 342 facilities, including Orotta Referral Hospital, working offline because of limited internet.
A 2024 DHIS2 conference abstract says a tracker module was added for patient-level data. Its reach is not verified.
About 20 percent of people used the internet in late 2025, which limits linked records.

clinical.summary: A treating doctor cannot see records held by other facilities, because no shared record or exchange exists. A 2018 Ministry of Information report quoted an IT technician calling nationwide connected hospital wards a future goal.
detail: Records are kept at each facility; a 2026 study abstracted medical histories from paper clinical cards.
DHIS2 carries aggregate statistics for planning, not clinical records for treatment.
No emergency access or cross-provider viewing rules were found.

research.summary: No law sets consent or opt-out rules for reusing health data, and data reuse rules are not verified. One safeguard counts: the Ministry of Health's Research Ethics and Protocol Review Committee approves studies, which report written consent.
detail: The 2010 National Health Policy commits to strict observance of ethical principles in research.
A July 2026 study reports approval by the ministry committee and written informed consent from each participant.
A 2016 review of national ethics guidance across Sub-Saharan Africa found none for Eritrea on collecting or reusing biological samples.
No opt-out or public register of secondary uses was found.

ai.summary: We found no rules for AI in clinical care: no AI law, no AI strategy and no regulator. A 2019 medical device registration guideline exists, but no AI or software rules were found.
detail: The Ministry of Health and WHO built a medical devices registration guideline in 2019 for the National Medicines and Food Administration.
The African Union's medicines programme says Eritrea has no National Health Act, only proclamations on drugs and private practice.
A June 2026 legal tracker found no AI law, AI strategy or AI regulator.

journeyNote: Facilities send aggregate counts to the ministry's DHIS2 system, mostly offline. Patient records are on paper and stay with each facility. No insurance claims system or e-prescription was found.
